copy.name: How to use a scientific calculator
copy.blurb: Get the order, brackets, DEG and RAD, powers, logs and % right, and reuse answers.
copy.title: How to use a scientific calculator
copy.lead: You have a sum with brackets, a power or a sine in it, and the answer has to be right. You will type it in the correct order, pick the right angle mode, and reuse results without retyping. It runs in your browser.
copy.result: A correct result for sums with brackets, powers, roots, logs and trig, with the last 20 kept in your history.
copy.note: Most wrong answers come from two things: a missing bracket, or the wrong angle mode. Check those two first.
copy.s1b: The calculator follows standard maths order: brackets first, then powers, then × and ÷, then + and −. So 2 + 3 × 4 is 14, not 20.
copy.s2t: Open the Scientific calculator on cv.cm
copy.s2b: Tap the keys or type with your keyboard. The result appears as you type. Enter or = finishes the sum, Esc clears it, and ^ makes a power.
copy.s3t: Add brackets where the order matters
copy.s3b: Write (2 + 3) × 4 to get 20. Put the whole top and bottom of a fraction in brackets: (2 + 6) ÷ (1 + 3) is 2. A bracket left open is closed for you at the end of the sum, so check that it closes where you meant. Check the expression usually means an extra ) or a missing number.
copy.s4t: Choose DEG or RAD before using sin, cos or tan
copy.s4b: The DEG / RAD button switches between degrees and radians. Angles from a triangle or a protractor are in degrees; formulas with π are usually in radians. sin(30) is 0.5 in DEG and −0.988 in RAD.
copy.s5b: xʸ makes any power (2^10 is 1024), √ is the square root, x! the factorial. log is base 10 and ln is base e. % only divides by 100: 200 × 10% is 20, but 200 + 10% is 200.1. For a price plus 10%, write 200 × 1.1.
copy.s6t: Reuse answers and copy the result
copy.s6b: Ans puts the last answer into the next sum. History keeps your last 20 sums; pick one to use it again. Copy result sends the answer to the clipboard, ready to paste.
copy.diagram1: Brackets change which part is worked out first.
copy.diagram2: The same sin(30) gives two answers: check DEG or RAD first.

faq.a1: The calculator is in RAD mode, so it reads 30 as 30 radians. Switch to DEG and sin(30) is 0.5.
faq.q2: What is the difference between log and ln?
faq.a2: log is base 10, so log(1000) is 3. ln is base e (about 2.718), so ln(e) is 1. For base 2 you can type log2(8), which is 3.
faq.a3: Here % always means divide by 100, so 10% is 0.1 and 200 + 0.1 is 200.1. To add 10% to 200, write 200 × 1.1 for 220.
faq.a4: The power is worked out before the minus sign, so it reads as −(2²). Write (−2)^2 to get 4.
faq.q5: Why do I get Too large or Not defined?
faq.a5: Too large means the answer is beyond what the calculator can hold: 170! works, 171! does not. Not defined means the sum has no answer, such as dividing by 0.

copy.name: How to use an online notepad
copy.blurb: Notes that save as you type. Open and download .txt files, and know where the note lives.
copy.title: How to use an online notepad
copy.lead: You need somewhere to put text right now, with no account or app. You will write a note that saves itself, open or download a text file, and learn the one thing that can lose it. The note stays in your browser and nothing is uploaded.
copy.result: A note that survives closing the tab, and a .txt copy on your device whenever you want one.
copy.note: The note lives in this browser on this device only. Download it before you clear browser data or change devices.
copy.s1t: Know where the note is kept
copy.s1b: The note is saved in this browser on this device, not on a server. So it never leaves your device, but it does not follow you to your phone or to another browser.
copy.s2t: Open the Online notepad on cv.cm
copy.s2b: Start typing. The page saves shortly after you stop and shows the time of the last save. Close the tab and come back: the note is still there.
copy.s3t: Set the view for what you are writing
copy.s3b: Under View, turn off Wrap long lines for code or logs, so one line stays one line, and turn on Monospace font to line up columns. The counter shows words, characters and lines.
copy.s4b: Open file loads a UTF-8 text file up to 1 MB into the note, replacing what is there; Undo brings the old note back for a few seconds. A file in another encoding is refused and your note is unchanged.
copy.s5b: Download .txt saves the note as a file on your device. Do this for anything you would be sorry to lose. Copy all puts the whole note on the clipboard to paste into an email or a document.
copy.s6t: Clear it, and undo if you change your mind
copy.s6b: Clear empties the note, and Undo appears for a few seconds to bring it back. If the page says this browser is not saving notes, you are probably in a private window: download before you close it.
copy.diagram1: Saved in this browser only: download a copy to take it elsewhere.
copy.diagram2: Wrap on suits writing; wrap off keeps each line of code or logs whole.

faq.a1: Yes. It stays in your browser's storage on this device and is not sent to cv.cm. Anyone using this browser profile can open the page and read it, so avoid it on shared computers.
faq.q2: Will I lose my note if I close the tab?
faq.a2: No. It comes back when you open the page in the same browser. It is lost if you clear site data for cv.cm, which is why downloading a copy is worth it.
faq.q3: Can I get my note on another device?
faq.a3: Not automatically, as nothing is stored online. Download the .txt and open it on the other device with Open file.
faq.q4: Does it work in a private window?
faq.a4: You can write there, but private windows discard storage when closed, and some block it completely. Download the note before you close the window.
faq.q5: How long can a note be?
faq.a5: Up to 1,000,000 characters, and files you open can be up to 1 MB. Very long notes can feel slow in the text box.

copy.name: How to write and preview Markdown
copy.blurb: Headings, bold, lists, links, tables and task lists with a live preview, then copy the HTML.
copy.title: How to write and preview Markdown
copy.lead: You have a README, a forum post or some notes to format, and want to see the result as you write. You will learn the marks you actually need, check them in a live preview, and take away Markdown or HTML. Nothing is uploaded.
copy.result: A formatted document you have checked by eye, ready as Markdown, a .md file, HTML you can paste, or an HTML file.
copy.note: Markdown is plain text, so it opens anywhere. Sites differ on extras such as tables, so check them where you will publish.
copy.s1b: # and a space make a heading (## and a space a smaller one). **Two stars** make bold and *one star* italic. A line starting with - and a space is a list item, and [text](https://example.com) is a link. Leave a blank line between paragraphs.
copy.s2b: The Markdown box starts with a short example of every mark, and Show example brings it back at any time. Replace it with your own text and read the result in the Preview box as you go.
copy.s3b: Separate table cells with | and put a row of dashes under the header; a colon in that row sets the alignment. - [ ] is an open task and - [x] a finished one. Add ~~two tildes~~ for strikethrough.
copy.s4b: Wrap a word in single backticks for inline code. Put three backticks on a line above and below a block, and the block keeps its line breaks. Tab indents a line; press Esc and then Tab to leave the box.
copy.s5b: Raw HTML shows as plain text and is never run. Only http, https, mailto, tel and relative links become links, so a link that stays as text has an address the page will not trust.
copy.s6b: Copy Markdown and Download .md give you the source. Copy HTML and Download HTML give the finished page code. The text also stays in this browser, so you can come back to it.
copy.diagram1: What you type on the left, what readers see on the right.
copy.diagram2: A row of dashes makes a table; brackets make a checklist.

faq.a1: A way to format plain text with simple marks such as # for headings and ** for bold. GitHub, Reddit, Discord and many note apps read it.
faq.q2: Which Markdown does this preview support?
faq.a2: CommonMark's common syntax plus GitHub tables, task lists, strikethrough and bare links. Other sites may render the extras a little differently.
faq.q3: Why does my HTML show as text?
faq.a3: Raw HTML is kept as text on purpose, so a pasted document cannot run code in the page or in the HTML you copy. Use the Markdown marks instead.
faq.q4: How do I add a line break?
faq.a4: End the line with two spaces for a line break, or leave a blank line to start a new paragraph. A single line break on its own may be joined up when rendered.
faq.a5: No. It is rendered in your browser tab and kept in this browser. Up to 200,000 characters can be kept.

copy.name: How to make a CSS gradient
copy.blurb: Pick linear, radial or conic, set the colours and positions, then copy the CSS or save a PNG.
copy.title: How to make a CSS gradient
copy.lead: You want a gradient behind a page, a card or a slide, and writing the CSS by trial and error is slow. You will pick a type, place the colours, and copy CSS that is ready to paste, or save an image. It runs in your browser.
copy.result: A CSS background rule with a solid fallback colour, or a PNG at 1080p, 1440p, portrait or square size.
copy.note: Text over a gradient has to stay readable at both ends. Test the lightest and darkest colours with the text colour you plan to use.
copy.s1b: Linear blends in a straight line and suits most backgrounds. Radial spreads out from the centre, like a soft glow. Conic sweeps around a point, like a colour wheel or a pie chart.
copy.s2t: Open the CSS gradient generator on cv.cm
copy.s2b: Pick the type under Gradient. Press a preset for a starting point or Random for ideas, and the preview updates straight away.
copy.s3b: For linear and conic, drag Angle: 0° points up, 90° points right, and 180° points down. For radial, choose Circle or Ellipse instead.
copy.s4b: Each colour has a position from 0% to 100%, and you can use up to 6. Add colour inserts one, and × removes it. Close positions make a sharp edge, and far-apart positions make a soft blend.
copy.s5b: Copy CSS gives you two lines: a solid colour for very old browsers, then the gradient. Paste them into your element's CSS rule. It works on any block with a size, such as body or a card.
copy.s6b: For slides and wallpapers, choose an Image size and press Save PNG. Sizes include 1920 × 1080, 2560 × 1440, 1080 × 1920 for phones and 1080 × 1080 for square posts.
copy.diagram1: The three types differ in the path the colours follow.
copy.diagram2: Each colour sits at a position on the line, and the CSS lists them in order.

faq.q1: Why does my gradient not show on the page?
faq.a1: The element probably has no height. A gradient fills the element's box, so an empty block is 0 high. Give it a height or some content; for a full page, set html and body to height 100%.
faq.q2: Why are there two background lines in the CSS?
faq.a2: The first is a solid colour, and the second is the gradient. A browser that cannot draw the gradient ignores that line and keeps the colour.
faq.a3: Both work, as a gradient counts as an image. background is shorter and also resets other background settings, so use background-image if you are layering it over other backgrounds.
faq.q4: How do I make a hard colour stripe?
faq.a4: Put two colours at the same position, for example both at 50%. There is then no room to blend, so the colour changes at a sharp line.
faq.q5: Why does the PNG look banded?
faq.a5: Very wide gradients between similar colours can show faint steps, because a PNG stores 256 levels per colour channel. Use colours further apart, or add a slight texture in an image editor.

copy.name: How to make fancy text
copy.blurb: Turn plain letters into bold, script, gothic and circled text you can paste, and know the limits.
copy.title: How to make fancy text
copy.lead: You want a bio, a username or a heading to stand out where the app gives you no font options. You will convert your text, copy one style and paste it, and learn where it does not work. It runs in your browser.
copy.result: Styled text that pastes into social bios, names and posts as ordinary characters, with no font to install.
copy.note: These are not fonts. They are separate Unicode symbols that look like letters, which is why they paste anywhere, and also why they have limits.
copy.s1t: Know what fancy text really is
copy.s1b: Unicode includes sets of symbols that look like bold, script or gothic letters, many first added for maths. Fancy text swaps each letter for one of those symbols, so the style travels with the text.
copy.s2t: Open the Fancy text generator on cv.cm
copy.s2b: Type in Your text. Every style updates below it as you type, from Bold and Script to Gothic, Circled and Upside down.
copy.s3t: Pick a style that stays readable
copy.s3b: Bold and Sans bold are the easiest to read. Script and Gothic suit a short name or a few words, not a whole paragraph. Keep the rest of your bio in plain text.
copy.s4b: Press Copy beside the style you want and paste it into the app. Check it after saving: an empty box or a question mark means that device has no symbol for that character.
copy.s5t: Expect other characters to stay the same
copy.s5b: Letter styles change only A–Z, a–z and, in some styles, digits. Chinese, Japanese, Korean and accented letters such as é have no matching symbols, so they stay as typed. Strikethrough and Underline add a line to every character, and Upside down reverses the whole text.
copy.s6t: Keep it out of the places where it hurts
copy.s6b: Avoid it for anything people need to find or hear. Search may not match 𝐜𝐚𝐤𝐞 with cake, and screen readers may skip the symbols or read out their long names. Leave your real name and key words plain.
copy.diagram1: The same word, but different Unicode symbols, not a font.
copy.diagram2: Letter styles change only A–Z, a–z and some digits; everything else stays as typed.

faq.q1: Why do I see empty boxes?
faq.a1: The device has no font containing that symbol. Older phones and computers are the most likely to show boxes. Try a more common style, such as Bold.
faq.q2: Does it work with Chinese or accented letters?
faq.a2: Letter styles do not: Unicode has styled forms for A–Z, a–z and digits, not for those characters, so they stay as you typed them. Strikethrough and Underline do work, as they add a line to each character.
faq.q3: Can I use it for my Instagram or TikTok name?
faq.a3: Display names and bios usually accept it, though it depends on the app and can change. Usernames normally allow only plain letters, digits and a few marks.
faq.q4: Is it bad for screen readers?
faq.a4: It can be. Screen readers may skip the symbols or read each one by its full name, which makes a sentence very hard to follow. Leave important information plain.
faq.q5: Do I need to install a font?
faq.a5: No. You are copying characters, not a font, so the text looks styled wherever the reader's device has the symbols.

copy.name: How to flip a coin online
copy.blurb: Settle it fairly, flip up to 1,000 coins, and read streaks without being fooled by them.
copy.title: How to flip a coin online
copy.lead: Two people need a fair decision, or a class wants to see how chance behaves, and nobody has a coin. You will agree the call, flip one coin or up to 1,000, and read the totals and streaks. It runs in your browser.
copy.result: A fair heads or tails, or a batch of up to 1,000 flips with totals, percentages and streaks, and a summary you can copy.
copy.note: Each coin uses one secure random bit from your browser, so heads and tails are equally likely and earlier flips do not matter.
copy.s1b: Say who has heads and what each side means before you flip, and that one flip decides. A decision made in advance is what makes the flip fair to everyone.
copy.s2b: Tap the coin or press Flip. Space and Enter also flip it. The face shown when it stops is the result.
copy.s3b: Choose 10, 100 or 1,000 under Coins per flip. All of them land together and the page shows how many came up heads and tails, which is handy for a probability lesson.
copy.s4b: Results add up every flip since the last Reset, so press Reset first to read one batch on its own. Expect close to half each, not exactly half: in 100 coins, anything from 40 to 60 heads happens about 96% of the time.
copy.s5t: Do not read meaning into streaks
copy.s5b: Longest streak and Current streak show runs of the same face. They look surprising but are normal. After five heads in a row, the next coin is still 50% heads.
copy.s6b: Copy results gives you a line with the totals to paste in a chat or a report. Last 100 coins shows the recent faces in order. Reset starts a new count.
copy.diagram1: Every flip is an even split: one bit, two equal faces.
copy.diagram2: The coin has no memory: after any run, the next flip is still 50%.

faq.q1: Is an online coin flip really fair?
faq.a1: Yes. Each flip takes one bit from your browser's secure random generator, so both faces are equally likely. Nothing is sent to a server, so the result is made on your device.
faq.q2: Are heads more likely after a run of tails?
faq.a2: No. Believing so is called the gambler's fallacy. Each flip is independent of the ones before, so the chance stays at 50%.
faq.q3: How long a streak is normal?
faq.a3: Longer than most people guess. In 100 flips, a run of 6 or more of the same face is usual, and that does not mean anything is wrong.
faq.q4: Why did I not get exactly 500 out of 1,000?
faq.a4: Exactly half is actually rare, at about 2.5% for 1,000 coins. Most results fall between 470 and 530 heads, and the share gets closer to 50% as the number of flips grows.
faq.q5: Can I use it for something serious?
faq.a5: It is fair for everyday decisions, games and teaching. If a draw has legal or money rules, follow the official process, since it may need a witness or an audit.

copy.name: How to tune a guitar
copy.blurb: Tune E A D G B E with your microphone, read flat and sharp, and always tune up to the note.
copy.title: How to tune a guitar
copy.lead: Your guitar sounds off, or it is your first time tuning. You will set up the tuner, play one string at a time, and turn the pegs until each is within ±5 cents. It listens through your microphone, and nothing is recorded or uploaded.
copy.result: All six strings in standard tuning (E A D G B E), each within ±5 cents of its note.
copy.note: New strings and big temperature changes make a guitar drift, so a second pass is normal, and new strings may need several.
copy.s1b: Standard tuning from the thickest string to the thinnest is E A D G B E. The thickest is low E (about 82 Hz), and the thinnest is high E (about 330 Hz), two octaves higher.
copy.s2t: Open the Guitar tuner on cv.cm
copy.s2b: Press Start tuner and allow the microphone when the browser asks. Instrument defaults to standard guitar. Move to a quiet room and hold the guitar close to the microphone.
copy.s3t: Play one string and read the meter
copy.s3b: Leave Auto on, then pluck one string and let it ring. The page shows the closest string's note and how many cents off it is. In tune means within ±5 cents; a cent is one hundredth of a semitone.
copy.s4t: Turn the peg the right way
copy.s4b: Flat means too low, so tighten the string. Sharp means too high, so loosen it. Turn slowly and pluck again, because a small turn moves the pitch quickly, especially on the thin strings.
copy.s5b: If a string is sharp, loosen it below the note and come back up. The string then holds its pitch better, because no slack is left at the peg. Do the same for all six strings.
copy.s6t: Check again, or change the tuning
copy.s6b: Pulling one string slightly changes the others, so go through them all again. If Auto jumps between strings, tap one to lock onto it. Instrument also has drop D, DADGAD, open G, bass, ukulele, violin and cello.
copy.diagram1: Thickest to thinnest: E A D G B E, each with its target pitch.
copy.diagram2: Left of centre is flat, right of centre is sharp, and ±5 cents counts as in tune.

faq.q1: Why does the tuner show a different note from the string?
faq.a1: Auto follows the closest string, so a string far from its target can read as its neighbour, and an overtone can do the same. Tap the string you want to lock onto it, then pluck softly and tune up gradually.
faq.q2: Why does the reading jump around?
faq.a2: Noise and other ringing strings confuse the pitch reading. Mute the other strings with your hand, pluck with the soft part of your thumb, and read it just after the first attack.
faq.a3: It is the standard pitch of the note A above middle C. Leave Reference A4 at 440 unless you are matching a piano or a recording tuned to something else.
faq.q4: Can I tune without a microphone?
faq.a4: Yes. Tap the string you want, then press Play reference to hear its note and match the string by ear. Listen for the slow beats between the two sounds, and turn the peg until they stop.
faq.a5: Every time you play. Check it again after you put on new strings or move between hot and cold rooms, because both change the tension in the strings.

copy.name: How to find the factors of a number
copy.blurb: Get all factors, pairs and the prime factorization, and see how the factor count is worked out.
copy.title: How to find the factors of a number
copy.lead: You need the factors of a number for homework, for simplifying, or to check whether it is prime. You will find them by hand for a small number, then read the full answer for any whole number up to 18 digits. It runs in your browser with exact maths.
copy.result: Whether the number is prime, its prime factorization, the number and sum of its factors, and every factor pair for numbers with up to 2,000 factors.
copy.note: A factor divides a number with nothing left over. Each factor comes with a partner, so you only need to test up to the square root.
copy.s1t: Find the prime factors by hand
copy.s1b: Keep dividing by the smallest prime that fits. 360 ÷ 2 = 180, ÷ 2 = 90, ÷ 2 = 45, ÷ 3 = 15, ÷ 3 = 5, and 5 is prime. So 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5.
copy.s2t: Open the Factor calculator on cv.cm
copy.s2b: Type a whole number or tap an example such as 97 or 1001. You can group digits in threes, as in 1,234,567. The answer updates as you type.
copy.s3b: The first line says whether the number is prime, and the table lists the Previous prime and Next prime. 97 is prime; 1001 is not, as 1001 = 7 × 11 × 13. 1 is neither, as it has only one factor.
copy.s4b: Prime factorization gives the compact form, and Written out repeats every prime: 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5. Every whole number above 1 has exactly one such list of primes.
copy.s5b: Factor pairs are two numbers that multiply to give yours: 36 is 1 × 36, 2 × 18, 3 × 12, 4 × 9 and 6 × 6. They are also every whole-number rectangle of that area, which is useful for layouts and seating.
copy.s6b: Add 1 to each exponent and multiply. 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5¹ has 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 factors, which is the Number of divisors shown. All factors lists them, showing the first 1,000 if there are more.
copy.diagram1: Split until every branch ends in a prime: 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5.
copy.diagram2: Each factor has a partner, and the pairs stop at the square root.

faq.q1: What is the difference between factors and prime factors?
faq.a1: Factors are all the numbers that divide it exactly: 12 has 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12. Prime factors are the primes that multiply to make it: 12 = 2² × 3.
faq.a2: No. A prime has exactly two different factors, 1 and itself, and 1 has only one. Keeping 1 out means every number has just one prime factorization.
faq.q3: How many factors does a prime number have?
faq.a3: Exactly two: 1 and itself. A number with an odd count of factors is always a perfect square, as its square root pairs with itself.
faq.q4: Why stop at the square root?
faq.a4: Factors come in pairs, one at or below the square root and one at or above it. If nothing up to the square root divides the number, it is prime.
faq.q5: How large a number can the calculator handle?
faq.a5: Up to 18 digits, with exact whole-number maths. If the number has more than 1,000 factors, the first 1,000 are listed, and the counts stay exact.

copy.name: How to find the LCM and GCF
copy.blurb: Work out the least common multiple and greatest common factor, and know which one you need.
copy.title: How to find the LCM and GCF
copy.lead: You are adding fractions, simplifying one, or working out when two schedules line up. You will learn which of the two you need, find it by hand with prime factors, and check it with exact maths in your browser.
copy.result: The GCF and LCM of 2 to 20 whole numbers, with the prime factors and, for two numbers, Euclid's steps.
copy.note: GCF is also called GCD or HCF, and they all mean the same thing. The LCM of two fractions' denominators is their lowest common denominator.
copy.s1b: Use the GCF to split into equal groups or simplify a fraction: 12/18 divided by 6 is 2/3. Use the LCM to find when things line up or to add fractions: buses every 12 and 18 minutes meet every 36 minutes.
copy.s2t: Open the LCM and GCF calculator on cv.cm
copy.s2b: Type 2 to 20 whole numbers separated by commas or spaces, or tap an example such as 8, 12. Do not use thousands separators, as a comma always starts a new number.
copy.s3b: Write each as primes: 12 = 2² × 3 and 18 = 2 × 3². GCF takes each shared prime at its lowest power, 2 × 3 = 6. LCM takes every prime at its highest power, 2² × 3² = 36.
copy.s4t: Use Euclid's algorithm for big numbers
copy.s4b: Divide the larger by the smaller and keep the remainder, then repeat with the divisor and the remainder. 18 = 1 × 12 + 6, and 12 = 2 × 6 + 0. The last divisor, 6, is the GCF. The page shows these steps for two numbers.
copy.s5b: For two numbers, LCM × GCF equals the two numbers multiplied: 36 × 6 = 12 × 18 = 216. That lets you get the LCM straight from the GCF. This shortcut does not work for three or more numbers.
copy.s6t: Read the result and copy it
copy.s6b: The page lists both results and the prime factors of each number. Coprime: Yes means the GCF is 1, so no prime divides all of them. For two numbers, the LCM is then their product; with three or more it can be smaller (6, 10, 15 has an LCM of 30). Copy result sends the answer to your clipboard.
copy.diagram1: Shared primes make the GCF; all the primes together make the LCM.
copy.diagram2: Each line divides by the last remainder until nothing is left.

faq.q1: What is the difference between GCF, GCD and HCF?
faq.a1: None. Greatest common factor, greatest common divisor and highest common factor are three names for the same number.
faq.q2: What are the LCM and GCF of 12 and 18?
faq.a2: The GCF is 6 and the LCM is 36. Check: 6 × 36 = 216, which is 12 × 18.
faq.q3: How does the LCM help me add fractions?
faq.a3: It gives the smallest shared denominator. For 1/12 + 1/18, use 36: 3/36 + 2/36 = 5/36.
faq.a4: Two numbers are coprime when their GCF is 1, such as 8 and 15. Neither has to be prime; they just share no prime factor.
faq.q5: Why did 1,500 turn into two numbers?
faq.a5: A comma separates numbers here, so 1,500 reads as 1 and 500. Type 1500 without the separator.
